prompt.context: Our client is a large Chinese conglomerate with a lot of cash on its hands. They decided to invest this money in a plant that, by the end of this year, will have a full production capacity of 8 million aluminum wheels annually. Management assumes that it will be able to sell 20% of its production in the domestic Chinese market.
prompt.question: The company hired Roland Berger to determine if it can sell the remaining 80% of its production to the US market, which is the largest vehicle market in the world. What do you think?

clarifying_info.q: How many vehicles are produced in the US each year?
clarifying_info.a: About 17 million vehicles are produced in the US each year.

clarifying_info.q: What share of US vehicles are equipped with aluminum wheels?
clarifying_info.a: About 70% of new US vehicles are equipped with aluminum wheels.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the aftermarket for aluminum wheels?
clarifying_info.a: There are about 85 million cars in the aftermarket, of which about 24 million are less than 5 years old. About 10% of used car owners whose cars are less than 5 years old buy aluminum wheels.

clarifying_info.q: How do OEMs select wheel suppliers?
clarifying_info.a: Most companies will select one supplier who will supply the aluminum wheels for the entire lifetime of a car model. Suppliers are usually selected 24 months before a new model goes into production and have stringent quality controls.

clarifying_info.q: Has the client considered markets other than the US?
clarifying_info.a: They thought about that as another option, but they would really like to work with just the US.

framework: 1. Quantify client supply: Calculate how many cars' worth of wheels the client needs to sell in the US (80% of 8M wheels = 6.4M wheels = wheels for 1.6M cars).
2. Size the US new car market: Estimate how many new cars are sold with aluminum wheels annually (17M x 70% = ~12M).
3. Size the US aftermarket: Estimate annual aftermarket aluminum wheel demand (24M eligible used cars x 10% = 2.4M sets).
4. Assess required market share: Determine what share of each market the client would need to capture to sell 1.6M sets.
5. Evaluate feasibility: Examine supplier-OEM relationship dynamics, lead times, quality requirements, and distribution options.
6. Recommend entry strategy: Based on feasibility analysis, suggest the most viable path (e.g., sub-contracting to existing US suppliers).

questions.prompt: How many sets of aluminum wheels does the client need to sell in the US market each year?
questions.guidance: Client produces 8M wheels/year. 20% sold domestically = 1.6M wheels domestically. 80% targeted at US = 6.4M wheels = 1.6M sets of 4 wheels (cars).

math.setup: Total production = 8M wheels. US allocation = 80%. Each car uses 4 wheels.
math.answer: Client needs to sell wheels for 1.6 million cars in the US annually.

questions.prompt: How large is the US new car aluminum wheel market?
questions.guidance: Multiply annual US vehicle production by the share equipped with aluminum wheels.

math.setup: US vehicle production = 17M/year. Share with aluminum wheels = 70%.
steps: New car aluminum wheel demand = 17,000,000 x 70% = 11,900,000 ≈ 12,000,000 sets/year
math.answer: Approximately 12 million new cars per year are sold with aluminum wheels.

questions.prompt: How large is the US aftermarket for aluminum wheels?
questions.guidance: Apply the 10% purchase rate to the pool of eligible used cars (less than 5 years old).

math.setup: Used cars less than 5 years old = 24M. Purchase rate = 10%.
math.answer: Approximately 2.4 million sets of aluminum wheels are sold in the aftermarket annually.

questions.prompt: What market share would the client need in each market to achieve its sales goal?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare 1.6M target to each market segment. The aftermarket share required (66%) is implausibly high for a fragmented market, pointing attention to the new car OEM market. Even in the new car market, 1.6M out of 12M is ~13%, which is significant but more plausible if supply agreements can be secured.

math.setup: Target = 1.6M sets. Aftermarket = 2.4M sets. New car market = 12M sets.
math.answer: Would need ~67% of the aftermarket (not feasible) or ~13% of the new car OEM market.

questions.prompt: Is it feasible to enter the US OEM (new car) market, and how long would it take?
questions.guidance: Strong answers surface: (1) OEMs select a single supplier per model for its entire production life; (2) suppliers are selected 24 months before production starts; (3) the client would likely need ~12 additional months just to get on a preferred supplier list, implying a ~3-year lead time before any OEM revenue. Since the plant is ready this year, the OEM channel is not viable in the near term.

questions.prompt: What entry strategy would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Given OEM channel barriers and aftermarket fragmentation, the best near-term path is sub-contracting production capacity to existing US aluminum wheel suppliers (Tier 1 suppliers already approved by OEMs). This allows the client to leverage its low Chinese manufacturing cost without needing its own OEM relationships. The trade-off is lower margins due to sharing profit with the intermediary supplier, but it is the most scalable near-term option.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should the Chinese company consider when assessing feasibility of entering the US aluminum wheel market?

categories.name: Market Access & Distribution
ideas: Selling directly to OEMs vs. through intermediary Tier 1 suppliers
Aftermarket distribution channels (auto parts retailers, online)
Need to establish US distribution infrastructure
Brand recognition/trust in the US

categories.name: Supplier-OEM Relationship Dynamics
ideas: Single-source supplier model means very hard to displace incumbents
24-month lead time for OEM supplier selection
Stringent quality certification requirements
Long-term model-life contracts limit churn

categories.name: Competitive & Cost Factors
ideas: Chinese manufacturing cost advantage vs. US domestic suppliers
Anti-dumping tariffs or trade barriers on imported auto parts
Currency exchange risk
Logistics and shipping cost from China to US

categories.name: Regulatory & Quality
ideas: US safety and quality standards (e.g., DOT regulations)
Certification and testing lead times
Liability exposure for defective wheels
Import duties and customs compliance

categories.name: Strategic Alternatives
ideas: Sub-contracting to existing approved US suppliers
Acquiring a US wheel supplier to inherit OEM relationships
Targeting the aftermarket as an entry point while building OEM relationships
Expanding to other export markets (Europe, South America) rather than concentrating on US

recommendation: The client should NOT attempt to enter the US OEM new car market in the near term, given the 2-3 year lead time required to become a qualified supplier and the plant being ready this year.

The most viable near-term path is sub-contracting production capacity to existing US Tier 1 aluminum wheel suppliers, leveraging China's cost advantage while bypassing the need for direct OEM relationships.
The aftermarket channel alone cannot absorb the required volume (would need ~67% share), so it should be a secondary channel at best.
risks: Lower margins from sub-contracting vs. direct OEM supply
Dependence on intermediary suppliers who may limit volume or extract margin
Trade/tariff risks if US imposes anti-dumping duties on Chinese aluminum wheels
Quality perception issues in the US market for Chinese-made components
next_steps: Identify and approach major US Tier 1 aluminum wheel suppliers as sub-contracting partners
Negotiate sub-contracting agreements that could transition to direct supply over time
Simultaneously begin the OEM qualification process (quality audits, certifications) to position for direct OEM contracts in 3+ years
Monitor US trade policy for any tariff changes affecting aluminum imports from China
